title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We present a fully preregistered, archived, paired experiment (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) evaluating whether a deterministic verifier pipeline (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered intent→configuration tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM-only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt-5-mini + deterministic validator). Execution used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one LLM call per task) producing model_calls_used = 200. Observed (confirmatory set): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0). Paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Because identical per‑pair candidates were used and the baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that augmentation reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this execution. We publish the complete preregistered run and artifacts, give an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of the testability failure, and provide concrete, archive‑supported recommendations to enable informative repeats (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration using the reserved exploratory set, and deterministic pilot checks).

sections.introduction:
Automating human intent → device configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises to speed routine NetOps and reduce operator load, but incorrect or misordered changes can cause outages and security exposures. A prevailing mitigation pattern is to augment LLMs with deterministic validators or sandboxed simulators in a generate–validate–repair pipeline so that proposed changes are checked before execution. Prior method proposals and prototypes argue such tooling can reduce explicit constraint violations, but reported gains depend strongly on the fidelity of verification tools and on evaluation semantics (how candidate generations are sampled and whether repairs are applied). This sensitivity motivates reproducible, preregistered paired experiments that measure the causal effect of adding a deterministic verifier to LLM‑based NetOps pipelines under controlled generation semantics.

We preregistered cand-2026-01-prereg-v1 to answer the operational question: How does deterministic tool‑augmentation (generate → deterministic verifier → optional repair) change the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial NetOps prompts? The preregistered primary estimand is the paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded minus baseline) measured on binary indicators produced by a deterministic sandbox validator and tested with an exact McNemar two‑sided test and paired bootstrap percentile confidence interval (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). The preregistration specified N=200 unique paired tasks, deterministic task generation, explicit adversarial prompt transforms, clear exclusion rules, and two permitted generation semantics: independent per‑arm generation (one LLM call per arm per task) and shared_initial_candidate (one shared LLM call per task scored by both arms). The executed run used the shared_initial_candidate semantics to conserve hosted model budget.

Key result: under the executed semantics the deterministic validator labeled every confirmatory candidate SAFE (baseline = 200/200; guarded = 200/200; n11 = 200). The resulting paired difference is zero with p = 1.0 and a degenerate 95% CI at [0.0,0.0]. Because the baseline unsafe rate was 0% and identical candidates were scored in both arms, the preregistered causal hypothesis was not testable in this execution. The remainder of the paper (1) documents the preregistered design and execution accounting, (2) diagnoses why the run was non‑informative for the primary estimand using archived artifacts, and (3) gives artifact‑grounded recommendations for informative repeats while preserving the original preregistration structure.
sections.related_work:
LLMs are being rapidly explored for NetOps and AIOps tasks including intent translation, configuration synthesis, diagnosis, and limited self‑healing; surveys and prototype reports synthesize these applications and emphasize both potential and safety concerns [1,2,3]. A commonly advocated architecture is tool‑augmentation: pairing a generative LLM with deterministic or rule‑based validators, simulators (e.g., sandboxed replay), or constrained executors to form generate–validate–repair or divide–verify–refine pipelines. Empirical reports and methodological proposals demonstrate that such pipelines can reduce explicit constraint violations on curated tasks, but gains are task‑dependent and sensitive to verifier fidelity and sampling semantics [4,1].

Work on guardrails, schema‑based tool interfaces, and secure agent orchestration highlights practical trade‑offs: stricter schemas reduce acceptance of unsafe proposals but may increase false refusals and operator workload if validators are incomplete or overly conservative [5,6]. Adjacent red‑team and adversarial evaluations underscore the need for ROC‑style diagnostics (false negative vs false positive trade‑offs) and for adversarial tuning of prompt transforms to expose verifier weaknesses [7]. Evaluation literature for agentic NetOps argues for workflow‑centred, replayable experiments with deterministic task generators and archived validator traces so results are reproducible and auditable [3,2]. Our study follows these principles by preregistering a paired estimand, using a deterministic task generator and sandbox validator, and archiving full execution and analysis artifacts for deterministic replay.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study preregistration (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) fixed the primary estimand as the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on binary SAFE indicators produced by deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Confirmatory testing used an exact McNemar two‑sided test with alpha adjustments for multiplicity when needed; paired bootstrap percentile CIs used 10000 resamples with seed = 1729. Sensitivity analyses for technical failures and alternative failure codings were preregistered.

Task generation and scope. A deterministic generator produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks constrained to single‑AS multi‑device topologies and limited configuration fields (admin, mtu, vlan). Each task included an initial_state, expected_final_state, and an explicit required_sequence describing safe change orderings. Tasks were deterministically seeded to permit replay. The preregistration specified an adversarial prompt transform family (templated obfuscations, negations, and contradictory phrasing) and reserved an exploratory calibration set (up to 50 tasks) to tune adversarial strength prior to confirmatory execution.

Pipelines compared. Baseline: accept the LLM candidate and score post hoc with the deterministic validator. Guarded: run the same candidate through the deterministic sandbox validator; the validator returns a deterministic valid flag and detailed violation lists. The guarded arm could invoke an automatic repair per the preregistration, but repair traces are archived and, for confirmatory episodes, repairs were not applied (repair_provider_trace = null in archived scoring artifacts), so the guarded arm reflected pure validation.

Generation semantics and model budgeting. The preregistration allowed independent per‑arm draws (two LLM calls per task) or shared_initial_candidate (one shared LLM call per task). The run executed under shared_initial_candidate to conserve hosted model budget; model_calls_used = 200 (versus up to 400 if independent draws had been used). This choice preserves task reproducibility but removes per‑arm generation stochasticity, making discordant paired outcomes possible only if repairs are applied or validator behavior differs between arms.

Scoring and analysis. Deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applied full_intent_constraint_validation to each candidate, emitting binary SAFE/UNSAFE flags and structured traces. Confirmatory binary outcomes were derived from validator.valid (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE). The paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor computed the 2×2 contingency (n11,n10,n01,n00), exact McNemar p‑value, and paired bootstrap CI (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). Preregistered missingness and exclusion rules were enforced (one automated retry per failed model call, deterministic replacement for flagged items, abort rules if >10% technical failures). Deterministic reconciliation and provider audits were recorded to certify no technical failures or nondeterminism occurred in the confirmatory run.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and reproducibility checks. The execution manifest records completed_episode_count = 400 (200 paired episodes), failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 200, consistent with shared_initial_candidate semantics and no retries. Provider audit logs confirm 200 completed hosted model calls and zero cache reuse across conditions. Deterministic reconciliation checks passed: complete_pair_count = 200 and no flagged contamination or nondeterministic verifier outcomes were observed. All execution and analysis artifacts required for replay are archived in the public bundle referenced in the Disclosure.

Primary confirmatory outcome. The deterministic validator labeled every confirmatory candidate SAFE: baseline SAFE = 200/200 and guarded SAFE = 200/200. The observed paired contingency is n11 = 200 (SAFE in both arms), n10 = 0 (SAFE guarded only), n01 = 0 (SAFE baseline only), n00 = 0 (UNSAFE in both). From these counts the paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) equals 0.0. The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0; the paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI is degenerate at [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000; bootstrap_seed = 1729). All numerical outputs are identical to the archived analysis artifacts (paired_contingency_table.csv and condition_summary.csv).

Representative diagnostic traces. Archived per‑task scoring JSONs demonstrate that for multiple sampled tasks the shared_initial_candidate content was identical across baseline and guarded episodes and that validator traces show violation_count = 0 and valid = true in each case. The repair_provider_trace fields are null for all confirmatory episodes, confirming that no repair‑induced candidate changes occurred and that the guarded arm performed only validation. The combination of identical shared candidates and universal SAFE validator outputs mechanically prevents discordant paired outcomes and therefore prevents the preregistered paired estimand from being informative under these execution semantics.

Exploratory reserve and ROC diagnostics. The preregistration reserved up to 50 exploratory tasks to estimate verifier ROC and refusal trade‑offs; that reserve was not consumed before the confirmatory execution and thus no exploratory ROC estimation appears in confirmatory artifacts. The absence of exploratory calibration preserved strict preregistration fidelity but left the run unable to empirically estimate verifier sensitivity to adversarial injections for this model and task family.
sections.discussion:
Root cause analysis. The non‑informative ceiling outcome arises from three archived, mutually supporting facts: (1) the run used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one LLM candidate per task shared by both arms), (2) deterministic_netops_validator_v5 labeled every sampled candidate as valid, and (3) no automated repairs were applied in confirmatory episodes (repair traces are null). Under those conditions, the paired contrast has no opportunity to produce discordant outcomes attributable to the presence of the validator, so the McNemar test is mechanically uninformative despite zero observed unsafe proposals.

Implications for confirmatory design. A paired estimator that attributes outcome differences to the presence of a validator requires per‑arm variation that could produce discordant pairs. Independent per‑arm generation provides that variation at the cost of additional model calls: in this study independent draws would have required roughly 400 model calls (two calls per task) compared with the executed 200 calls. When hosted model budget constrains selection of generation semantics, the estimand must drive budgeting: if the primary goal is to measure causal effect of a verifier, independent per‑arm draws or repair‑enabled guarded arms are necessary.

Artifact‑grounded recommendations for informative repeats. All suggestions below are derived from the preregistration and the archived execution/accounting artifacts:
- Use independent per‑arm generation for the confirmatory paired contrast unless the guarded arm will deterministically alter candidates via repairs. The additional model call budget required is explicit in the preregistration accounting and the execution manifest.
- Consume a preregistered exploratory reserve (we allocated up to 50 tasks) to calibrate adversarial transforms until a baseline unsafe rate matching the power assumptions is observed. Archive calibration runs and freeze transform parameters before confirmatory execution to preserve preregistration validity.
- If repairs are enabled in the guarded arm, instrument and archive repair_provider_trace artifacts and report the fraction of UNSAFE→SAFE conversions; analyze whether repairs introduce new violations. In our confirmatory artifacts repair traces are null, so repairs did not serve as a discordance mechanism.
- Run a deterministic pilot check on a small holdout to detect ceiling/floor contingencies before committing to the full confirmatory test; if the pilot yields no discordant pairs, follow a preregistered contingency‑preserving adaptation (for example, switch to independent draws or strengthen adversarial transforms) rather than proceeding with an uninformative test.

Alternative estimands. When budget or policy preclude independent per‑arm draws, consider alternative estimands that remain testable under shared semantics: estimate the absolute unsafe‑proposal rate of the LLM baseline with CIs; treat the guarded pipeline as an accept/reject gate and estimate refusal and post‑repair SAFE rates (requires repair application and traces); or use exploratory ROC estimation based on adversarial injections. These alternative analyses are enumerated in the preregistration and map to different resource trade‑offs.

Threats to validity and external generalization. The synthetic task family restricts changes to admin/mtu/vlan and single‑AS topologies; the deterministic validator encodes full_intent_constraint_validation for this restricted family. Thus zero unsafe detections here should not be interpreted as production safety across multi‑vendor, multi‑AS, or richer configuration domains. Additionally, only a single model (declared gpt-5-mini) and one deterministic validator were evaluated; multi‑model or multi‑validator generality is not established. Finally, operator workload and false‑refusal trade‑offs remain unmeasured because no guarded refusals occurred in the confirmatory set.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived, preregistered paired experiment comparing baseline LLM generation and a deterministic validator‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). This ceiling outcome made the preregistered causal hypothesis untestable in this execution. The principal contribution is methodological and reproducibility‑centred: (1) a complete deterministic preregistered run with archived artifacts permitting exact replay; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the run was non‑informative for verifier efficacy; and (3) concrete, artifact‑supported design recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration via the exploratory reserve, and deterministic pilot checks) for informative repeats. Researchers and operators planning similar confirmatory contrasts should budget generation semantics to match the estimand and use the archived artifacts to avoid repeat design pitfalls.

Topic constraints and autonomy boundary: the human Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) prior to the autonomy lock; after the lock the autonomous researcher performed literature review, preregistration (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1), experiment design, code generation, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, autonomous peer review, and revisions. Preregistration and execution: the preregistration froze the estimand (paired SAFE‑rate difference), paired design N=200, deterministic task generator, allowed generation semantics, scoring rules, and stopping rules; these elements are archived in the preregistration artifact. Executed generation semantics and model‑call accounting: independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate semantics) producing a single initial LLM candidate per task shared across arms; model_calls_used = 200 while the preregistered maximum_model_calls for independent per‑arm generation = 400. Validator and scoring: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performed deterministic sandboxed validation and encoded outcomes as binary labels (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE) under scoring_rule = full_intent_constraint_validation; archived scoring JSONs contain validator traces showing validation_before/after and violation lists. Repair status: in confirmatory episodes repair_provider_trace entries are null, indicating no automatic repairs were applied in the confirmatory scoring. Analysis executor: paired_binary_analysis_v1 computed the paired contingency, exact McNemar two‑sided test, and paired bootstrap CI (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes were executed; the observed model call count reflects the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics. Reproducibility pointers: full execution and analysis artifacts (execution/* and analysis/*) are archived in the supplied bundle and permit deterministic replay. Human editing: no manual human edits to technical content, analyses, or manuscript text occurred after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock development: infrastructure rehearsals occurred prior to the lock but were excluded from final empirical evidence unless reproduced under the post‑lock execution.
limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies and limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or explicit injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
